title: Freddie Hunt on his father James’ ‘incredible’ 1976 title
excerpt:
James Hunt was a larger-than-life character endowed with an undeniable charisma, but of course his greatest triumph was winning the 1976 Drivers’ Championship by a single point over his dear friend and rival Niki Lauda, which happened 50 years ago today.

For the latest instalment of F1 Icons, his son Freddie – who, like his father, found an immense love for motorsport – looks back on that remarkable season and the legacy Hunt built…

Unfortunately, in 1976 they didn't have the footage like they do now. Imagine if they had modern technology in those days – it would've been a joy to watch. I've seen as much as I can, and I've read an awful lot about it.

That year would be considered an incredible season in any sport, just the drama of it. Dad was a complete underdog there, in that no one knew how quick he was because he had never had a team mate in Formula 1 before.

To jump in the McLaren and get pole position in the first race in Brazil… I don't think Jochen Mass liked it very much because he thought he ought to be the number one driver. And of course, Niki qualified alongside him, which really summed up that whole year.

All the ups and downs of it and Dad's relationship with Niki came together to make it an unforgettable season. Most of the drivers got on very well because you had to respect one another on the track in those days, otherwise you’d end up killing your mate or getting yourself killed.

But it was wonderful and exciting – I can't imagine how incredible it would have been for the motorsport enthusiasts.

I've tried to put myself in their shoes, like I was seeing it from a spectator's point of view. As an enthusiast, it would've been the most brilliant, gripping season of all.

I think it was also one of the greatest comebacks in the history of the sport in terms of points – I searched it and he was 17 points behind Niki with three races left, so that alone made it one of the most dramatic, for sure.

But it’s the last race in Fuji that sticks out to me, particularly because it seemed like Dad didn't know where he was. He had to change tyres when not everyone else did, and I actually think he messed that race up!

He made a mistake by not cooling his tyres, but I don't know, maybe the other guys were all on a harder compound. You do see them driving through the puddles to cool them down, and Dad didn't do that. I reckon it was just too much adrenaline and focus, I guess, but who knows?

50 years since the iconic season that inspired ‘Rush’

Other than that, the US and the Canadian Grands Prix stand out to me too. The pressure was off at that point and he wasn't thinking about the championship because he had just lost the points from the British Grand Prix.

Therefore, I think he just sort of threw caution to the wind, and that was it. He enjoyed the racing, won both the races and created a possibility to win the championship.

I think he drove very well in the second half of the season. He did in the first half too, but in the second he got his confidence, he got his rhythm, and his consistency improved, no doubt. He really stepped up to the mark when it mattered.

There’s no other way to describe his rivalry with Niki than as a great, exciting one. It's horrible when two rivals don't like each other, when they're at each other's throats. That's sad to see.

Dad and Niki were very good friends. When they were close to one another on the circuit… I'm not going to begin to speculate what was going through their minds at the time, but I imagine it was very difficult, and different to what’s going through two drivers' minds nowadays.

I didn’t know Niki particularly well. I only spoke to him a few times, mostly on camera actually, but there is a great story about their friendship. Before they reached F1, Dad got arrested and Niki went to bail him out.

This was in Germany or Austria, so Niki spoke the language, and I think this was when they raced in F3. He told the police: “No, no, you can’t arrest him. He can't spend the night – he's racing against me in the morning. You've got to let him out!”

I don't know how I’d sum up his legacy. He's fondly remembered, he is. I’m incredibly proud and I can't think of what other adjectives really – it’s just pride. I’m impressed by what he could do, and I have a tremendous amount of respect not just for him, but for all of those drivers in those days because it was absolutely lethal.

All I can say is he was kind, he was considerate, and he was respectful. Several people have told me that one of his lovely characteristics was that he could be at a dinner table with the Queen on one side and the binman on the other, and he wouldn't talk to them any differently.

When he was excited he could be volatile, as I'm sure you've seen from footage of him getting out of the car. On the other hand, he could be excited in a social environment and become terribly mischievous.

Someone once said they were waiting for a bus, the bus never came, and I think there were three of them. They had no alcohol, no nothing, pouring down with rain. They were sheltering in this bus stop, waiting for the bus which never came, but somehow Dad made it fun.

title: Sainz 'not expecting miracles' after Williams struggle in US
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has admitted that Williams are “not expecting any miracles” after a disappointing start to the United States Grand Prix weekend in Austin.

The Spanish driver finished 19th in FP1 and 20th in FP2 and was more than 2.7 seconds behind Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, who topped both sessions.

His Williams team mate Alex Albon faced even bigger problems and struggled to keep his car on the track, finishing bottom of the timesheets on the day.

There was clearly plenty of frustration on show between the pair as they battled away in the dry Texas heat, with Sainz heard on the team radio admitting that his car was a “mess” and that he had “no confidence” in it.

Speaking to the media after FP2, Sainz gave an honest reflection of the team’s performance and what they are expecting from the remainder of the weekend’s sessions.

He said: “We know that we’re pretty much nowhere to be seen this year and we’re braced for a tough weekend.

“We’ll try to learn as much as possible which might give us some information for the future, but we’re not expecting any miracles going into the weekend.”

Asked whether the team’s focus had already shifted to testing parts and strategies for 2027, Sainz agreed but was also adamant that Williams had an important task to achieve with this season’s car first.

“More than parts for next year is mapping this year’s car properly,” he added. “We need to know why it is so bad. We’re going to understand what to do better for next year.”

That opinion was shared by Paul Williams, Chief Trackside Engineer for Williams. He supplied a deeper assessment into the difficulties both Sainz and Albon faced and explained what lessons the team can take away from Friday’s practice sessions.

“We spent most of today learning and looking at the future, so you saw a bit of a different programme for us in FP1. That was very much forward-focused, both for the remainder of this year, but really looking into next year.

“We've got to find that balance between performing here on this race weekend and the remaining races this season but also looking forward to the performance for next year's car.

“[COTA] is one of the easiest overtaking tracks, if not the easiest, so we'll be focusing more on high fuel long run performance and finding that correct balance between the low fuel qualifying pace and high fuel. That's really going to be our main focus and extracting that from the FP2 data.”

title: Hadjar rues ‘undriveable’ Red Bull in Austin
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar described his second practice session in Austin as “a disaster” and his Red Bull RB22 as “undriveable” after struggling to set a representative lap time on the soft tyre.

Hadjar finished the session in P9 and a huge 0.931s behind team mate Max Verstappen, who took third spot behind Charles Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli.

Hadjar struggled particularly with his tyres after set-up changes were made between the sessions, with the fronts overheating through the high-speed corners early in the lap and leaving him short of grip thereafter.

“We had an okay FP1, and then in FP2 I felt okay as well on the medium, even though we changed the car,” he said. “And the soft, honestly, the car was completely gone for me. So yeah, very difficult to drive.

“I need to turn things around tomorrow, sit down and see what we can do, because the car made a massive step down. We need to bring it back at least to the level it was this morning.”

Hadjar added: “It's just a disaster. After Sector 1, basically, where I made most of my lap time, from Sector 1 to the end of the lap, I was slower than on the medium.

“It was just undriveable, and I was losing the front end massively. So we need to have a look, because that's not normal, why there's so much deg on one lap.”

Verstappen, meanwhile, did not encounter the same level of difficulty after a power steering change following an issue in FP1. While Hadjar confirmed that there were some set-up differences between the cars, he remained hopeful that changes for Saturday will help.

“Yeah, if they managed to do it on the other side [of the garage],” the Frenchman said. “It's like the temperatures are going sky high, and we're going at the same speed.

“So we need to tweak something on the car balance, because we're running different stuff. You need to try. But to have such a bad feeling, I'm a bit surprised, to be honest.”

Red Bull Technical Director Pierre Wache confirmed the team had gone in the wrong direction with Hadjar’s car, while stressing that its set-up was not drastically different from Verstappen’s.

“Well, I think it's an overall set-up direction that we have to undo, between P1 and P2, and it's what we are working on this evening,” Wache said. “They are not far away. With this type of layout, you have the full high-speed corner during the Sector 1, after Turn 1, and I think if you overcook the tyre there, after it's more or less finished for the lap.”

Wache indicated that COTA’s bumps were proving challenging for the RB22.

“As expected it's jumping a lot,” he said. “The problem with this type of setup we are using, that is quite not as stiff as last year but not so far, is that the car is not very compliant on these bumps here.”

Wache concluded: “It's clearly the low speed performance where we are focused on at the moment – low speed is the key for us.”

title: What the teams said – Friday in the United States
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from Friday practice at the Circuit of The Americas ahead of the United States Grand Prix.

Oct 24, 2026 12:29am UTC

Ferrari

Charles Leclerc topped the opening practice session for Ferrari, starting strongly at a track where he has previously won. Lewis Hamilton was close to his team mate on the mediums, but ran wide on his first flying lap on the softs to finish a few places further back. It was much of the same for the team in FP2, Leclerc setting the pace and Hamilton a little further back. One thing that did cause some raised eyebrows was Leclerc nearly tangling with Russell as both squabbled over the same piece of tarmac, the stewards later opting to take no further action.

Charles Leclerc - FP1: 1:36.052, P1; FP2: 1:35.291, P1

"The feeling in the car was quite good. Our upgrades worked as expected, but we must not get carried away by too high expectations ahead of tomorrow, as I believe our competitors have more potential to unlock. Kimi (Antonelli) and Max (Verstappen) already look very strong, and they’ll definitely be up there in qualifying. We’ll keep our heads down and see what tomorrow has in store."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:36.555, P6; FP2: 1:35.906, P4

"It wasn’t the easiest day. We tried a different direction with the set-up, but I wasn’t comfortable in the car, especially over the bumps. Charles showed there’s pace there, so we need to understand how we can get the car into a better place on my side. Practice is always a good opportunity to try new things and build our understanding and we’ll work through it with the team tonight and see where we can improve for tomorrow."

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Charles Leclerc of Monaco driving the (16) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain driving the (44) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images)

Mercedes

George Russell complained in FP1 about his brakes, while Kimi Antonelli found himself in a spot of bother after getting in the way of Hadjar. Both ran wide on occasion too, as they like most of the field, struggled for grip. The Italian found things more to his liking in FP2, although he did need a trip back to the garage to adjust his seat, which was moving in the cockpit of his Mercedes. He wound up less than half a tenth off the pace of Leclerc, while Russell was a little further back after having a hairy moment on one of his laps, catching a big snap that could have been nasty.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:36.533, P5; FP2: 1:35.333, P2

"We have had an interesting day here at the Circuit of the Americas. We didn’t have the best FP1 session, with the car balance not in a great place. We were able to improve that for FP2 though and we took a good step forward. We will now pick through the data overnight and see if we can take another step. We will likely need that if we are to be confident of fighting for victory on Sunday.

"Ultimately, it’s been an encouraging day for us given the progress we’ve taken with the update package. We made some good inroads in Singapore, and it is pleasing to see that continue here with both myself and George on the same specification. There is still more for us to do to ensure we’re getting the car in the right window consistently and that will be a focus for us heading into FP3."

George Russell - FP1: 1:36.378, P4; FP2: 1:35.793, P5

"It's been a useful day for us on track as we continue to build our knowledge around our update package. Whilst the car wasn't in a great place in FP1, we made some good improvements for FP2 and definitely moved the car in the right direction. There is still more work to do though, particularly given how strong some of the other teams looked today. I didn’t get the most out of the single-lap running either; I lost one lap to track limits and then had a big moment in sector one on the next, so there was more performance there. We’ll work hard overnight and see what we can find ahead of tomorrow.

"As we expected coming into the weekend, the margins between the top four teams look small. Getting ourselves in the fight at the front will not only be about making improvements with the car overnight but also executing well in qualifying and the race."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We didn’t have a good first session. We were looking to explore a wider set-up window with the update package on both cars, but we were struggling with locking, which was a big limitation in both our single-lap work and the long runs. We repositioned the cars going into the afternoon session and that seems to have put us in a better place. We had fewer balance issues, the car was more predictable, and the lap times improved as a result.

"It looks very tight at the front. You wouldn’t rule out any of the top four teams having the pace for pole position tomorrow, so we’ll continue to pick through what we learned today and see if we can find further improvements overnight."

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team cools down in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Red Bull

Max Verstappen started well in Austin, briefly topping FP1 but losing his fastest time to track limits. Fortunately, his previous lap was good enough for P2 as he pushed Leclerc close. Isack Hadjar also lost a soft-shod lap time to track limits, which sent him tumbling down the order. The Dutchman started the second session well in his Red Bull machine, looking strong once again and is definitely in the mix for pole. Hadjar once again struggled a little by comparison, calling his laps “disgusting” on the radio at one point. The Frenchman will be studying the data tonight to see if he can find any answers ahead of the final practice session.

Max Verstappen - FP1: 1:35.860, P2; FP2: 1:35.480, P3

“It’s been a positive start to the weekend. This track is never easy when it comes to finding the right compromise between the low and high-speed corners. The bumps make it even more difficult, so you’re trying to find a good balance in the car and get into a rhythm. That’s what we’ve been working on between FP1 and FP2. There’s still a bit more work to do to fine-tune that balance, but it wasn’t a bad day at all.”

Isack Hadjar - FP1: 1:36.490, P14; FP2: 1:36.411, P9

“We started today well in FP1. The track was as bumpy as expected, but we took some learnings from that. For the second session we then made some changes. They didn’t go as we’d hoped, as we struggled on the Soft tyre compared to the Medium. The first sector was good, but after that, we had issues with tyre temperature for the rest of the lap. There are things to improve and work on overnight, particularly with the car balance, which should help. We have Fridays for a reason, so let’s push on tomorrow.”

Pierre Wache, Technical Director

“The set-up we are running is less stiff than last year, but the car is still not compliant enough over the bumps, which made today quite challenging as finding the right balance was more difficult than expected. The main challenge this weekend is managing tyre degradation over the long runs while making sure the compromises we make for race pace don’t cost us too much in Qualifying. We had a steering issue on Max’s car in FP1, which we managed to resolve, and we saw some improvements with the set-up in FP2. There is still work to do on both cars, particularly Isack’s, but we are not far away in terms of set-up. With the high-speed corners in Sector 1, pushing the tyres too hard early on can compromise the rest of the lap. We are focused on improving our low-speed performance and, while the race is our priority, we also want to put ourselves in the strongest possible position for Qualifying.”

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands and Oracle Red Bull Racing prepares to drive during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

McLaren

Lando Norris was the pick of the two McLaren drivers in the opening session, with Oscar Piastri struggling with understeer on his fast lap. Come FP2, it was Norris who struggled more with the car, unable to find the best working window. He had a moment on his flying lap, and was not particularly complimentary about the car after the session. Piastri looked a little more steady in FP2, but he was not that quick, so the Australian will be hunting lap time tomorrow.

Lando Norris - FP1: 1:36.297, P3; FP2: 1:36.373, P7

“We saw encouraging signs of pace today, but it’s been tough to repeat that lap after lap. We’re focusing on small, targeted tweaks overnight rather than anything drastic to get on top of the car’s handling. We’ll use everything we’ve learned through both sessions today to put the car in the best position we can and make it a little nicer to drive before Qualifying.

“Compared to the teams ahead we’re a step behind. It’s not a drivability issue as such, it’s focusing on extracting speed consistently because the pace is definitely there. We’re optimistic that incremental changes will bring us closer in the competitive order.”

Oscar Piastri - FP1: 1:36.786, P7; FP2: 1:36.029, P8

“An interesting first day for us. It’s clear that we have a bit of time to find on track. We tried a few different things during the sessions that we now need to fully analyse to see how we can better maximise performance from the car. The main thing we’re struggling with is grip, so we have work to do on that side of things. We’ll see what we can do overnight to get us in a better spot ahead of Qualifying tomorrow.”

Rob Marshall, Chief Technical Officer & Chief Designer

“We’re relatively satisfied with how the day went. The balance of power amongst the top four teams is quite close – closer than the FP2 standings suggest, a session in which we clearly didn’t maximise our potential. The long runs were quite positive, and the series of minor updates we’ve brought to this track seem to be delivering the expected results in terms of performance.

“This is a circuit with a number of medium and high-speed corners that suit our car’s characteristics, but there are also plenty of low-speed sections, an area we’re working on intensively.

“Ferrari seem to be very strong, as is Max Verstappen, who is really strong here, and Mercedes are also competitive: for our part, we’ll try to make the most of the data collected today to challenge these teams."

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Oscar Piastri of Australia and McLaren looks on in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

Arvid Lindblad has taken a new ICE and thus will have a grid penalty on Sunday. He wound up in the top 10 in the first session, a couple of tenths ahead of his team mate. The rookie dropped down the order in the second session, but Liam Lawson went the other way, topping the midfield with an impressive lap. That bodes well for the Racing Bulls team, but they did have one interesting moment, watching the Kiwi racer go wheel-to-wheel with Verstappen out of the pits as those two got a taste of racing a little earlier than planned at COTA.

Arvid Lindblad - FP1: 1:37.063, P9; FP2: 1:36.734, P13

"It's a really cool track here in Austin, and I've definitely enjoyed driving it thanks to its great flow. Overall, it's been a day of ups and downs. We made a good start in FP2, although I struggled a little to find the rhythm on the Soft tyre. Our pace on the short runs has been good, but we still have some work to do on the long runs. We've identified a direction to follow, which will hopefully help us find more performance. A big thank you to everyone in the team for the incredible work they're putting in and for bringing the new upgrades this weekend. I'm looking forward to building on today's work and making further progress over the rest of the weekend."

Liam Lawson - FP1: 1:37.309, P10; FP2: 1:36.331, P6

"I enjoyed being on track today. We've brought some upgrades this weekend, so the car is feeling quick, and I believe there's still more to unlock with some fine tuning. There's definitively more degradation than we expected, but it normally comes down throughout the weekend, so we'll assess what it's like tomorrow. I love driving here, so am looking forward to Quali where we'll be pushing for Q3."

Alan Permane, Team Principal

"It’s been a good day. We have a new aero package on the car, comprising a new floor, bodywork and front and rear wings on both cars, which is working as expected. We can make some improvements to the balance of both cars overnight, but the numbers look encouraging overall. Our pace for both short and long runs look decent, so it will be small tweaks for FP3 tomorrow. The track presents a few challenges, with the hot temperatures leading to more tyre degradation than we’d like, while track limits can also be tricky here. It’s easy to get it wrong, so I’m sure that’ll be a topic both in Qualifying and during Sunday’s race. Arvid does have a five-place engine penalty this weekend due to a new internal combustion engine. However, we’re not changing his run plan; the objective, as always, is to qualify as high as possible. We’ve got a little bit of work to do overnight to ensure we’re in a strong position tomorrow."

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Liam Lawson of New Zealand driving the (30) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain driving the (41) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Audi

Gabriel Bortoleto was fast in FP1, winding up the pick of the midfield. His Audi team mate could not match him, Nico Hulkenberg struggling with a power unit issue and forced to park up a little early at the end of the first session. The German was also down the order in the second session, while Bortoleto spent much of the afternoon flirting with the top 10. Unfortunately for him, he has a back of the grid start incoming after taking on a raft of new PU components.

Nico Hulkenberg - FP1: 1:38.122, P18; FP2: 1:37.040, P18

“Today was a pretty straightforward Friday without any issues. We tried a few things across FP1 and FP2 and learnt a bit along the way. Now it’s about going through everything and putting a good plan together for qualifying tomorrow. The midfield looks tight, as ever, so hopefully we can get ourselves in the mix for a good starting position."

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP1: 1:36.995, P8; FP2: 1:36.832, P11

“Overall, it was a regular day in the office. We had two clean sessions, with decent pace, and we got quite a good amount of data on how our car is performing here. Of course, knowing we'll have a grid penalty puts us in a slightly different position going into the rest of the weekend, as we already know we will be starting from the back, which is obviously a shame especially when the car feels good. But that is part of the game, and I am still confident we can do a decent job and get the most out of qualifying tomorrow.”

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Nico Hulkenberg of Germany driving the (27) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Alpine

Franco Colapinto had a stop-start beginning to his weekend, confined to the garage in the opening stages of FP1. He finished a couple of places behind his team mate, with Alpine keeping their powder dry in the first session. The Argentine has a 10-place grid drop incoming for taking on a new PU component too, which will hamper his weekend. As for Pierre Gasly, he improved a few places from one session to the next, but needs to find a few more tenths if he wants to fight for Q3 tomorrow.

Pierre Gasly - FP1: 1:37.801, P15; FP2: 1:36.840, P12

“From a results point of view, it does not look to be the best day for us but we know some areas we can improve and I am sure we will still be in the mix for the top ten when it matters. The track is very bumpy, usual for here as it's the nature of the track, and it has been quite difficult to get a good read on car balance. A lot of our set-up work has been trying to get the car riding better over the bumps. We are probably not as strong here as we would like to be, so we have quite a bit to learn and understand overnight. Our pace on high fuel in Free Practice 2 was better, which is obviously very important with an eye on Sunday. That being said, we still need to qualify as high up as possible, and I am sure much of our work in Free Practice 3 will be on improving our single lap pace. Finally, it was the first time for me doing an interview live from the car with Sky Sports F1 in Free Practice 1, that was quite cool and hopefully gives those watching on TV a slightly different insight into racing than usual!”

Franco Colapinto - FP1: 1:38.121, P17; FP2: 1:37.201, P15

“We had a busy day out on track today with a lot of focus and preparation for Sunday and long runs. It was similar in a way to the approach we took in Malaysia, where we also knew we would be taking a grid penalty. Therefore, we did not do much performance running or Qualifying simulations and took the sensible decision to put ourselves in the strongest possible position for the Grand Prix. We will work with the engineers tonight and debrief on what we learnt on my side, as well as Pierre's, and see where we can take a step forward as I think there's still some margin to improve. Also, like Sepang, but to a lesser extent, this track can be tough on tyres and degradation will play a part in the race. We have seen in past races that following in dirty air can also emphasise that more, which is again why we shifted focus more towards race set-up. It's a fun track to drive and we will give it our all tomorrow to start as high up as possible.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“It has been a tricky Friday for us and we have quite a bit to improve going into the rest of the weekend. We had both cars running slightly different programmes as a result of Franco having to take a grid penalty due to taking a new control electronics unit. Franco's day mainly focused on completing plenty of laps and lots of high fuel running to give him a good read for the car in race trim. We know overtaking opportunities are more abundant here so all is not lost for Franco if he can have a strong start on Sunday and put himself back into the mix to score points. Pierre had a more conventional Practice programme, trying different set-ups and trying to get the car into a better place, especially over some of the bumps which are a big characteristic at this circuit. He's not as comfortable on low fuel as we'd like, so that gives us an area to focus on and improve. On high fuel we look stronger, which bodes well for Sunday, but is opposite to a trend of ours from recent races where we tend to be strong on low fuel. That is something we need to work on and understand ahead of tomorrow as we aim to continue our streak of Q3 appearances.”

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Pierre Gasly of France driving the (10) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Franco Colapinto of Argentina driving the (43) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images)

Haas

Ollie Bearman was the pick of the two Haas drivers in the first session, with the team running a special Godzilla livery at their home race. The same held true in FP2, with Bearman just sneaking into the top 10 by a couple of tenths, with team mate Esteban Ocon claiming 14th. That bodes well for Haas, who have not made it to Q3 since China. Whether Bearman can hold the position when everyone turns things up remains to be seen, but it shows that the upgrade direction Haas have gone in does seem to be paying dividends.

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:37.665, P11; FP2: 1:36.536, P10

“It’s been a positive first day in Austin. I had a good feeling in the car, and to be honest, it’s been a continuation from Singapore in terms of that good feeling, so that’s nice. There are a few things we’ll look at tonight to be able to get some more performance out of the car, but we’ll see what we can do for qualifying – I’m optimistic!”

Esteban Ocon – FP1: 1:37.896, P16; FP2: 1:37.201, P14

“Conditions are good out there, but the track is quite bumpy all the way around. We’ve struggled since the start of the day, front-locking everywhere, and the car’s very difficult when trying to attack the corners. We’ve changed a few parts compared to Singapore, so we need to understand where that’s coming from. We’ll keep looking tonight and hopefully come back better tomorrow.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“I think it was a reasonably successful Friday. On Ollie’s side, he was happy with the car straightaway and had lots of confidence, so that’s probably the cleanest Friday of the season from his side of the garage so far. On Esteban’s side, it’s not a huge problem, but he’s struggling under braking – so we need to get to the bottom of that issue. If we can, I’m sure we can get Esteban up there with Ollie. The competition is really tight, so it’s about fine-tuning, and we really need to squeeze everything out of it tonight to be in the best position for FP3 and qualifying tomorrow.”

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Oliver Bearman of Great Britain driving the (87) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari is returned to the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Simon Galloway/LAT Images)

(Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Aston Martin

Aston Martin had a strong opening session in Texas, Fernando Alonso winding up just outside the top 10 and Lance Stroll only one place and one tenth back. Alonso was the pick of the duo again in FP2, although he was not impressed with traffic in the form of Russell at one point. Stroll once again wound up one place adrift of the Spaniard, although the time gap came down to just 0.034s in the second session as the Canadian began to stretch his legs around this rollercoaster of a circuit.

Fernando Alonso - FP1: 1:37.688, P12; FP2: 1:37.235, P16

Lance Stroll - FP1: 1:37.783, P13; FP2: 1:37.269, P17

Stroll said:

"We worked through our testing programme and focused on improving the car throughout the day.

"I think we're looking a little better here than we did in Singapore, although we're still down on power on the straights. We seem to be a bit stronger through the corners, so there are some positives.

"Getting out of Q1 is going to be tough, but you never know what can happen.

"We'll go through the data tonight, look at where we can make adjustments and see if we can improve the car ahead of Qualifying."

Team Ambassador Pedro de la Rosa said:

"We have both cars close to one another in lap times today, and we completed everything in our programme across both FP1 and FP2.

"All in all, it was a good Friday for us, but there is still some work to be done to improve the balance on the car.

"Track limits will be a key factor tomorrow in Qualifying, as we've seen lots of laps deleted today. It's the same for everyone and we'll see what we can do tomorrow."

(Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Cadillac

Colton Herta ran in place of Sergio Perez in the opening session in front of his home fans, but his session had a tricky start. He kept it clean though, handing over an intact Cadillac to the Mexican for FP2. Perez was a little late to come out as the team finalised setting up his car, and understandably took some time to get going. He wound up a couple of places behind his team mate, Valtteri Bottas with the Finn putting in two solid sessions at a track where he has tasted victory.

Valtteri Bottas - FP1: 1:39.053, P20; FP1: FP2: 1:38.422, P19

“A productive Friday for us here in COTA with no issues. We were able to conduct some interesting tests with a couple of different front wings and various set-ups too. It's been a really smooth day that has allowed us to learn the best we can and try to find the optimal window.. It still looks like there is a bit of a gap to the others, so we’re going to do our best overnight to try and find something to help us improve.”

Sergio Perez - FP2: 1:39.036, P21

“It was a busy session, especially given that I missed FP1. We had a lot to get through, including experimenting with a few different parts and set-ups on the car, so we learned a lot. One of the changes we made probably put us on the back foot for the rest of FP2, but we understand why and know what we need to do overnight to be in better shape tomorrow. The team has done a fantastic job, and Colton also provided some really useful feedback.”

Colton Herta – FP1: 1:39.979, P21

“That was fun. My first Formula 1 outing in my home country in front of all the American fans was a very special moment. We’ve got a lot of people here from Cadillac and GM, so it was amazing to be able to share that with them too. It’s been great to be back at COTA - it’s been seven years since I was last here when I won in INDYCAR, so it’s surreal to be back on track here, this time driving a Formula 1 car.”

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“Colton did a very solid job in FP1, completing our program and providing valuable data for the rest of the weekend. This was his third FP1 appearance and that growing familiarity with the car is helping him get up to speed more quickly and give increasingly useful feedback to the engineers.

“With Checo and Valtteri we ran our test items including the floor elements and that will prove useful for the future. We’ve had a positive day and we will work overnight to get ready for Quali tomorrow. At this track we need to focus on getting the best set up and optimising the tyre window.”

Williams

Williams ran a test programme in FP1, and thus their times were not representative. They were also the only team not to run the soft tyres. Alex Albon’s flying lap was deleted as he fought his car around the Circuit of The Americas, and thus he wound up propping up the field. The second session did not improve for the team, Albon and Carlos Sainz seemed to lack confidence with the car. They both ran wide, with Albon once again unable to set a representative lap time.

Alex Albon - FP1: 2:16.468, P22; FP2: 1:43.426, P22

“That’s Friday finished with and it was a tricky day overall. We utilised FP1 to do an aero testing programme to gather data for both this season and to help the development of the 2027 car. Currently there’s a lot of work to do, and a lot to debrief overnight, but let’s see what the rest of the weekend brings.”

Carlos Sainz - FP1: 1:38.846, P19; FP2: 1:37.701, P20

“We knew it was going to be a tough circuit for us; the medium to high speed longer corners just don’t suit our car, so we chose to use FP1 to try different setups and gather some data which will help us to prepare for next year. For FP2 we went back to a normal run plan and unfortunately the performance struggles proved to match the expectation. Having said that, the weekend is only getting started and we will continue to dig into the data and try to improve as much as possible for both qualifying and the race."

Paul Williams, Chief Engineer - Trackside Performance

“We spent most of today learning and looking to the future, working as a team to collect some data both for the remainder of the season but also very much looking forward to next year’s car and our development programme on that. We know the limitations of this car and struggle on the medium- and high-speed corners so are exposed here in sector one, but this is one of the easiest circuits to overtake on so the focus for us this evening will be making sure we have got the car underneath us for long runs and can keep rear tyre degradation under control on Sunday."

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Carlos Sainz of Spain driving the (55) Williams FW48 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

AUSTIN, TEXAS - OCTOBER 23: Alexander Albon of Thailand driving the (23) Williams FW48 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of United States at Circuit of The Americas on October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Pirelli

Dario Marrafuschi, Pirelli Motorsport Director

“The indications from the first two sessions confirm very consistent behaviour from the three compounds selected for this Grand Prix. So far, the C2 appears likely to play only a limited role in defining race strategies, while teams are focusing primarily on the Medium and Soft compounds. Given the level of degradation observed and the rapid evolution of track grip, a one-stop race currently appears to be the most likely scenario.

"Track evolution is progressing as expected. The surface was particularly dirty at the start of running, but it rubbered in quickly, allowing grip levels to reach a very good standard. The performance gaps between the compounds are also in line with expectations, at around nine tenths of a second between the Medium and Hard, and five tenths between the Medium and Soft. Particular attention will also be paid to the aerodynamic balance of the cars, an aspect made even more significant by the bumps and irregularities of the track surface. An imbalance can increase the tendency for front-wheel locking under the heaviest braking zones, making it crucial to find the best possible compromise in terms of car set-up.”

title: Leclerc warns against ‘high expectations’ at US GP
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc revealed that Ferrari “need to be careful” despite topping the times in FP1 and FP2 at the United States Grand Prix, hinting that their upgrades aren’t as impactful as some may believe.

The Scuderia have made changes to key aerodynamic components including the floor, sidepod inlet and diffuser, which Lewis Hamilton predicted would only deliver “half a tenth” in performance during Thursday’s press conference.

Leclerc nevertheless managed to set the pace in the first two Free Practice sessions at the Circuit of The Americas, albeit by slim margins of 0.084s and 0.042s over Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli respectively.

The Monegasque was reluctant to get his hopes up for the rest of the weekend, as he explained: “The feeling is quite good but we need to be careful – obviously it’s only Friday.

“We are seeing what we expected but again, it’s definitely not what everybody thinks in terms of upgrade and lap time gained. It’s been a good day. I think the balance of the car was good and straightaway, we started in a good window. That paid off.

“Obviously all the hard work that has been done in order to bring this upgrade as soon as possible is also helping us a little bit, but we shouldn't carry too high expectations going into tomorrow. I feel like the others have more potential to unlock.

“Kimi and Max seem to be very strong. The McLaren, I don’t really know yet. I don’t think they put everything together, but Kimi and Max will definitely be up there.”

Although the gap between the top four teams has narrowed as the season has progressed, Ferrari haven’t won a race since Round 9 in Great Britain, and Team Principal Fred Vasseur was just as keen as Leclerc to remain realistic about their chances this weekend.

“It’s a good start, but I think once again it’s very tight,” he said. “I’m not sure that the classification of FP1 was always relevant for Qualifying.

“It means we have to be focused on ourselves to continue to work. We have a lot of things to learn on the car with the new package, and try to do a better job tomorrow.

“It’s a very early stage. For sure the impact [of the upgrades] is a bit less than at the beginning of the season. It means that we have to finetune everything and try to get the best for tomorrow.

“Let’s see Qualifying first because as soon as you’re in the dirty air, it’s more difficult. I think that we have five or six cars that can compete for pole tomorrow. It’s good for F1 and it’s good for us if we’re in front.”

title: Why Norris found it 'very difficult' to maximise the McLaren
excerpt:
Lando Norris has cited the McLaren car's handling issues as the reason behind their challenging Friday in Austin, despite the signs of decent pace it displayed during practice.

Amid all the talk ahead of the United States Grand Prix weekend about the pecking order between the top four teams one thing became clear on Friday – McLaren was in a clear fourth place at the end of FP2.

While just 0.189s covered the three different cars in the top three, with Charles Leclerc edging out Kimi Antonelli and Max Verstappen, there was a huge gulf of 1.082s from the pacesetting Ferrari to Lando Norris in P7, with Oscar Piastri just 0.014s behind in P8. The fact that both papaya cars lost out to the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson was a further indication that things hadn’t gone to plan for the Woking team.

However, as is often the case, the headline times didn’t tell the true story as there were also signs of decent pace from the MCL40. The problem was that it proved hard for the drivers to complete a representative lap as they struggled with handling issues.

“It's difficult,” said Norris after the session. “I think the pace is not bad. We seem to step away from Red Bull and Ferrari, probably Mercedes as well. So, we seem a little bit off comparing to them.

“But the car is just very difficult to drive, like it has been for a long time, too difficult to be able to be consistent and to get a nice feeling consistently. The pace is not bad, it's just very difficult to achieve it.”

Expanding on his struggles, the reigning champion said: “Just to get the car to be quick, we're just a step behind. So to get the car to be quick, we have to try so hard to be perfect, and you cannot be perfect.

“I mean, I'm sure everyone has similar problems in a way, but we're just not quick enough yet easily to be there consistently.”

Despite the issues, Norris remained hopeful that set-up changes overnight will improve the situation and McLaren could find a way forward through the remainder of the weekend.

“I think we just need to make some small tweaks to the car,” he said. “It's not like there's anything crazy.

“It's just... it's tough, and maybe at the minute our car handling is just a little bit on the difficult to achieve side, so maybe small things in a few directions can help us out. But the pace is there or thereabouts so we can still be optimistic.

“Of course, we're putting the car in the best position we know we can at the minute. But we'll see what we've learned from today, what we can improve on, what little tweaks we can do, what can move it in that direction to make it a little bit nicer to drive. And we'll go again.”

Also speaking after the session, Chief Technical Officer and Chief Designer Rob Marshall had a more optimistic perspective and believed that McLaren can still be in the fight with their main rivals on Saturday.

“I think we will,” he said. “We set a purple in P2 as well. We just didn't finish the lap. It was a competitive lap up until the point where we made a mistake.

“Okay, we made mistakes, but yeah, that was just one lap. I think going forward from here, we've got to be quite optimistic, really.”

Also on the plus side for the Woking-based squad was that a small package of upgrades, focused on revised front and rear “corner furniture” and the diffuser, worked as intended.

"Yeah, we're very pleased actually,” said Marshall. “I wouldn't say it’s a tiny upgrade, but it's really small parts that are kind of almost a bit of tuning, really. But they seemed to deliver quite well, so certainly a measurable benefit, and we think we see it in the stopwatch as well. So yeah, we're quite pleased.

“They were sort of test items, which we never really planned to race. But there was a secondary part of that brake stuff, which was really an aerodynamic gain, and sort of conditioning around the wheels and wake control, that sort of stuff. So we think that's delivered for us.”

title: Palmowski closes in on title with Opening Race victory
excerpt:
Alisha Palmowski put one hand on the 2026 F1 ACADEMY title as she secured her fifth win of the campaign in the Opening Race in Austin.

The Red Bull Racing driver overcame opening lap drama, losing the lead off the line to Payton Westcott. However, a poor Sector 1 from the Mercedes driver opened the door for Palmowski to retake the position at Turn 9.

Contact between Rachel Robertson, Rafaela Ferreira and Megan Bruce necessitated an early Safety Car, with Palmowski holding firm on the restart. Behind her, Alba Larsen overtook team mate Nina Gademan and chased down the Briton for the lead. However, the Ferrari driver was eventually told to give the place back after completing the move off-track.

Out front, Palmowski held firm despite a second Safety Car restart on the final lap to take the victory and extend her lead to 63 points, with Alpine junior Gademan and Ferrari’s Larsen completing the podium.

Lisa Billard claimed her best result of the season in fourth ahead of title contender Emma Felbermayr. Natalia Granada was sixth, followed by Payton Westcott, who dropped to seventh after a mistake following Palmowski’s opening lap overtake.

Esmee Kosterman finished eighth in the LEGO Racing car ahead of Ella Stevens, while Williams’ Jade Jacquet took her first points in the series in P10.

With this victory, Palmowski could be crowned Champion in Saturday evening’s Reverse Grid Race, which takes place at 1800 local time. The Briton will line up in P8, one place ahead of her nearest rival Felbermayr. Her Campos Racing teammate Rafaela Ferreira will be hunting down her maiden podium, as the Racing Bulls driver goes from Reverse Grid pole.

title: Esteban Ocon exploring potential F1 lifeline at rival team after Haas axe
excerpt:
Esteban Ocon and his management team are trying to find a way to secure a race seat in F1 for 2027 after his axe by Haas.

Esteban Ocon and his team are exploring the possibility of him securing a race seat at Cadillac in 2027, but to have a chance, a major change needs to be made.

The French driver leaves Haas at the end of this season after two years, but there are few landing spots for a 2027 race seat available.

Only Racing Bulls and Mercedes have yet to officially confirm their 2027 line-ups, along with the Haas team Ocon is leaving.

But Racing Bulls is facing its own 'three-into-two doesn't go' dilemma over Liam Lawson, Arvid Lindblad, and Nikola Tsolov, whilst Kimi Antonelli and George Russell will remain at Mercedes.

One potential possibility for Ocon is Cadillac, where he enjoys good relations with new team principal Marcin Budkowski, from their time working at Alpine together between 2021 and 2022.

Sergio Perez is understood by RacingNews365 to be a key pillar of the Cadillac project.

Perez has performed at a very high level in his comeback year, especially in comparison to his team-mate Valtteri Bottas, seemingly putting the Finnish driver’s seat at risk.

Paddock sources have suggested that it can be considered a sign of Bottas' situation that his manager, Didier Coton, is on-site in Austin for the United States Grand Prix this weekend - a home race for the team where all the key decision-makers are in attendance.

RacingNews365 understands, however, that the team's immediate position is to focus on this season and decide about a potential change late on if needed.

Ocon and his management team are understood to have reached out to Cadillac to discuss the possibility of the one-time grand prix winner taking the seat.

But it is understood that the team is very cautious at this stage, particularly after already making a significant change this year when Graeme Lowdon was axed as team principal in the summer break in favour of Budkowski (below).

[Article continues below with Budkowski's response on the future of his driver line-up]

© XPBimages

Cadillac address future of F1 driver line-up

The future of Cadillac's driver line-up was put to Budkowski in the Friday team principal's press conference in Austin, where he did not completely rule out the possibility of a driver change.

Asked specifically about links to Ocon, Budkowski told media, including RacingNews365, that: "As a team principal, and I’m sure it’s the same with my colleagues, you’re getting calls and contacts from every driver or driver manager that is on the market.

"So, there are a number of drivers and managers who have contacted me. I’m not going to say who it is or who it isn’t, but pretty much all of them that are on the market have been in touch, as you’d expect.

"But I think it’s the last place [here in the press conference], as you can imagine, where I would communicate anything on the driver line-up. My marketing and communications department would kill me if I did that."

When then directly questioned on whether Bottas and Perez have contracts for 2027, Budkowski did not directly answer the question.

"Again, this is the last place I would comment on driver contracts, and in general, I think it’s not something that is done in the press," he said.

"It’s something which will be done by official releases from the team when the time is right."

Next weekend's Mexican Grand Prix is Perez’s home race and his 300th grand prix in Formula 1, seemingly providing the ideal opportunity for the team to confirm his seat for next season.

While Bottas’ place is in question, several paddock sources are saying that Cadillac’s American owners are still considering Colton Herta as a potential option.

At the same time, RacingNews365 understands that, as well as Ocon, other drivers are also trying to explore a potential opportunity at Cadillac. One of them is Yuki Tsunoda.

On Friday, paddock sources suggested that Liam Lawson's team is also in touch. The New Zealand driver is still not confirmed at Racing Bulls as the team deliberates on whether to promote Tsolov. It is understood these talks are nothing more than exploratory at this stage.

Should Ocon not be on the grid for 2027, another potential destination would be the third and reserve driver role at Aston Martin, with Ocon keen to resume his grand prix career in 2028.

title: Kimi Antonelli rise branded 'hell of a story' ahead of potential F1 title party
excerpt:
Nico Hülkenberg has described Kimi Antonelli's rise to the top of F1 as "a hell of a story", with the Mercedes driver in a position to seal the title at this weekend's United States Grand Prix.

Antonelli leads the drivers' championship by 102 points ahead of team-mate George Russell, and could be crowned the youngest champion if he wins at the Circuit of the Americas, provided Russell finishes ninth or lower and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fifth or lower.

It marks a remarkable turnaround from a difficult rookie campaign in 2025, when Antonelli struggled to adapt, notably scoring a miserable three points across the nine grands prix in Europe.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, in Austin, asked how special Antonelli's season has been given his age, Audi driver Hülkenberg replied: "Very, very impressive.

"He's had a hell of a year, and a hell of a turnaround story from 12 months ago, where things looked very difficult and very different for him.

"It just goes to show how things can change so rapidly in this business, in this industry, and it all goes back to the feeling and your confidence with the car and with yourself.

"It's quite astonishing, a hell of a story, and respect, fair play to him. He's been pretty flawless this year, pulling off some incredible performances. Very impressive for his age."

Asked whether it was astonishing that Antonelli had managed such a turnaround, Hülkenberg pointed out the context behind it.

"Well, obviously it's his second season that he's doing it, not his debut season, but still, it is very astonishing, a huge achievement, and huge respect for what he's doing," added the German.

Mercedes has brought an aerodynamic and chassis upgrade package to Austin for both cars, following performance shortfalls identified in Malaysia and Singapore, as the Brackley-based squad looks to give Antonelli the tools to finish the job in Texas.

title: Colton Herta closing in on F1 superlicence as magic points tally within reach
excerpt:
Colton Herta is closing in on finally earning his F1 superlicence, but he still remains two points away from finally achieving it after his latest FP1 outing.

Herta took over Sergio Perez's Cadillac for his fourth FP1 outing of the year on Friday of the United States Grand Prix, and has now moved to what RacingNews365 has calculated as 38 superlicence points, with 40 required to obtain the document to enable him to potentially race in F1.

However, a Cadillac team spokesman, when asked by RacingNews365, indicated that Herta was on 39 points following the Austin session, but did not answer when asked where this extra point had been added to Herta's tally.

The simplest method for Herta to achieve his superlicence, with the maths to get to the magic 40-point mark, is explained below.

One point from 10th place in 2023 IndyCar standings

30 points from 2nd place in 2024 IndyCar standings

Four points from 7th place in 2025 IndyCar standings

This brings Herta to 35 superlicence points.

The American can then add three points achieved in the Barcelona, Austria, and United States FP1 sessions he completed as he racked up over 100km in running.

Herta also took over Perez's car in Italy, but he only completed five laps of Monza for 25km of running, and therefore does not earn a 39th point as this was below the required 100km.

He can achieve his superlicence by the end of the year if Cadillac use him in at least two more free practice sessions, one of which is mandatory, as Valtteri Bottas has only missed one FP1 session for Herta thus far, with each regular race driver being required to miss two sessions.

When asked about the possibility of Herta taking over the MAC-26 for more sessions between now and the end of the season to get to the 40-point mark, the same team spokesman added that it would be "remiss to not give him the opportunity to secure his superlicence."

[Article continues below]

Herta addresses latest superlicence point situation

After his outing at Austin, Herta spoke of his commitment to still making it to F1 with Cadillac, as soon as possible.

"It is super important to pick up the points when I can," Herta told media, including RacingNews365.

"I hope [I'll be in the car again], and I think we're still figuring some stuff out with the team, and they'll have a better idea.

"To be honest, I don't know where I am at [in terms of superlicence points]. I've spent so many years thinking about it and worrying about it that I let other people do it for me.

"My goal is still to be in Formula 1, and the goal is to get there as soon as possible with Cadillac, with GM, with TWG, and this is where I want to be.

"So I am focused on trying to get here as soon as possible."

title: Lewis Hamilton pledges Ferrari overhaul after making wrong F1 decision
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has pledged to work with his Ferrari engineers to ensure his car is using the correct set-up after a mistake on Friday in Austin.

During Friday practice for the United States Grand Prix, team-mate Charles Leclerc topped both sessions, the first time a Ferrari has done so in 2026, with Hamilton sixth in FP1 and then only fourth in FP2.

He was 0.503s and 0.615s slower in the two sessions, respectively, although he did not set his quickest FP2 lap on the first lap of the soft tyre run after a mistake at Turn 1 forced him to abandon the effort.

Reflecting, Hamilton described how the bumpy nature of the Austin circuit had not left him "comfortable" in the SF-26.

"It wasn’t the easiest day," Hamilton began.

"We tried a different direction with the set-up, but I wasn’t comfortable in the car, especially over the bumps.

"Charles showed there’s pace there, so we need to understand how we can get the car into a better place on my side.

"Practice is always a good opportunity to try new things and build our understanding, and we’ll work through it with the team and see where we can improve."

title: Isack Hadjar receives 'left-field' instruction to close Max Verstappen chasm
excerpt:
Juan Pablo Montoya has told Isack Hadjar to consider going "left-field" to try and close the chasm to Max Verstappen in United States GP practice.

Verstappen placed second and third, respectively in the two sessions on Friday in Austin, with Hadjar placing 14th and ninth, respectively.

In the two sessions, the Frenchman was 1.654s and 0.931s slower than the Dutchman, respectively as Verstappen continued his recent strong momentum, whilst Hadjar slipped back at a track Verstappen has only been beaten at once in any race format since 2019 - when Charles Leclerc won the 2024 grand prix.

Hadjar himself labelled the day as a "disaster", the car as "undriveable" and said he was "completely killed in the high-speed corners."

Analysing the situation, six-time grand prix winner and two-time Indy 500 victor Montoya believes that Hadjar faces two options to close the gap to Verstappen, one of which is a risky "left-field" option.

"The thing is, as the season's progressing and he wants something different out of the car, it makes it harder because all the development, all the simulation, everything is based on what Max wants," Montoya observed on F1TV.

"So you're coming here with more of an unknown car and a car that is a little bit out of your window. So it makes it really hard.

"Yes, you can do all your own work, but then the rest of the work that gets done is all focused on what Max is looking at, and it's working. So they're not going to change it because they're winning the races.

"So you're not going to change it, so you have two options: you either adapt a little bit to what Max wants, or you go completely left field and try to explore the car in a different way.

"That's really hard because if you don't perform, they start questioning: 'What are you doing? Why are you going this way? It's not working. You need to get back.'"

[Article continues below].

Hadjar's troubled Friday in Austin

Continuing his analysis, Montoya added that he hoped there was a technical issue with Hadjar's car to further explain the huge chasm in Verstappen's pace.

"And you go back, and you still can't drive the car. So it's not easy.

"I feel bad for him, but I mean, he's got a ton of talent. He's got a ton of speed. So I don't know, I'm hoping that there's an issue, to be honest."

title: Niki Lauda 'hands' F1 rival world championship glory with stunning decision
excerpt:
It is perhaps F1's greatest forgotten title decider coming in a season which itself is perhaps overlooked in the absolute all-time great debates.

1976 had McLaren going at it with old rivals Ferrari, contentious disqualifications, the reigning world champion nearly dying in pursuit of his defence, and a showdown at the first-ever Japanese GP for the ages.

October 24th marks exactly 50 years - half a century since the 1976 Japanese Grand Prix - the day James Hunt defeated Niki Lauda in one of the most astonishing title deciders of all-time.

1976 title decider

After the trials and tribulations of 1976 that included Hunt being disqualified from a win at Brands Hatch and Lauda receiving the last rites, twice, after his horrifying accident at the German Grand Prix, and missing two races, the title race boiled down to a showdown at Fuji.

Coming into the race, Lauda had 68 points to Hunt on 65, in the days of the top six scoring points in the 9-6-4-3-2-1 system.

Essentially, it meant that if, for whatever reason, Lauda failed to score any points, Hunt was required to finish third or better to take the title.

As race day dawned in Japan, the heavens opened and the torrential rain forced a delay whilst drivers even debated about taking the start.

Eventually, they did, but on the second lap, in a act of defiance, Lauda pulled into the pits and retired, claiming that "my life is worth more than a title" - as Ferrari tried to encourage him back into the race - one two-time world champion Emerson Fittipaldi would also soon withdraw from citing the conditions.

But Hunt ploughed on, and looked set for an easy win until the track started to dry and his tyres fell away, prompting a late pit-stop, in which he fell to fifth, two places below where he needed.

On Lap 71 of 73, Hunt overtook both Alan Jones and Clay Regazzoni to haul himself into the magical third place - as he sealed the most astonishing of titles to become Britain's sixth world champion after Mike Hawthorn, Graham Hill, Jim Clark, John Surtees, and Jackie Stewart by just one point over Lauda.

The race itself was won by Mario Andretti who was now taking F1 seriously with Lotus, the big story, one which would, of course, become a Hollywood film with Rush in 2013 was Hunt vs Lauda - one of the greatest rivalries in F1 history.

Having climbed to the top of the mountain, Hunt dropped off in 1977 as Lauda wrestled his title back, and by mid-1979, both had retired from grand prix racing, although Lauda would be tempted back in 1982 for a four-year spell, at McLaren of all places, which yielded the 1984 title.

To this day, Lauda remains the only driver in F1 history to win the drivers' world championship for Ferrari and McLaren.

title: McLaren hand F1 rivals warning over hidden Lando Norris potential
excerpt:
McLaren CEO Zak Brown believes Lando Norris was "much quicker than we looked" in United States Grand Prix practice - after making a mistake.

Norris only placed seventh in the second practice session at Austin, and was 1.082s slower than pace-setter Charles Leclerc, with Liam Lawson even squeaking ahead in the Racing Bulls machine into sixth place.

However, on his best lap time, Norris made a mistake in the final sector of the lap, ruining his strong pace in the first two, which could have led to a more representative lap time ahead of final practice and qualifying.

Reflecting on the performance, Brown explained that had Norris been able to execute a perfect lap, the MCL40 would have been "there or thereabouts."

"I think Lando is definitely a lot quicker than his lap time [suggests]," Brown told Sky Sports F1.

"He didn't get his third sector in, and his first two sectors were very strong, so I think we are much quicker than we looked.

"I think Ferrari's lap time, Mercedes' lap time, we're there or thereabouts."

The team's chief technical officer and chief designer, Rob Marshall, then added that the team had reason to feel optimistic.

"We set a purple [sector] in FP2 as well, but just didn't finish the lap," said Marshall.

"It was a competitive lap up until the point where we made a mistake.

"I think it's going forward from here, and we've got to be quite optimistic, really."

[Article continues below].

McLaren upgrades verdict

Then turning to the upgrades McLaren had delivered to Austin, Marshall explained that whilst the parts had worked, they were not intended to be raced.

"We're very pleased, actually," he said.

"We bought a few... I wouldn't say as a tiny upgrade, but it's really small parts that are kind of almost a bit of tuning really. But they seem to deliver quite well, so there is certainly a measurable benefit.

"We see it in the stopwatch as well, so we're quite pleased.

"They were kind of test. They were test items which we never really planned to race. But there was a secondary part of that brake stuff that was really an aerodynamic gain and conditioning around the wheels and weight control, that sort of stuff. So we think that's delivered for us."

title: Max Verstappen offers sharp and unusual Christian Horner book 'review'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen said he does not read books when asked for his thoughts on Christian Horner's autobiography Drive, released earlier this week.

Verstappen skirted around the question, providing a sassy response before revealing he had no intention of digging up — or addressing — the past, following the publication of the former Red Bull team principal's reflections on his time in motorsport.

Unsurprisingly, the four-time F1 drivers' champion features numerous times, given the success he shared with Horner.

However, the 29-year-old was uninterested in correcting or validating the record, ignoring the suggestion that long-time ally Helmut Marko opposed his promotion to Red Bull from Toro Rosso in 2016.

Asked whether he or his father, former F1 driver Jos Verstappen, had read the book and what his thoughts on the contents were, the Dutchman was in no mood to entertain the question.

"Why me and my dad? Not my mum or my sister?" Verstappen quipped back to media, including RacingNews365.

Put to him that it is because Verstappen and his father are both referenced quite a bit, he responded, "Because we've worked together for a very long time, right?"

Addressing the question fully, he said: "Well, I haven't read the book. I don't read books, to be honest, myself.

"But also, for me, there is also no need for me to sit here and say, 'Well, this is correct; that's not correct; I think this; I've seen differently'.

"Those things have all happened in the past. We've had a great time all together, right? I mean, our relationship has lasted for such a long time together working here. But for me, what is now very important is what is happening right now, here."

[Article continues below]

Where Verstappen's attention really lies

Building on his eyes-forward mentality, Verstappen underlined his main desire to enjoy racing and tackle the immediate tasks at hand, continuing his race-winning form and returning to title contention next season.

"I'm focusing on this weekend. I'm focusing on next year. I'm having a good time within the team," he added, as he prepares to attempt to take victory for the third successive grand prix.

"Over time, of course, yeah, people have changed; they have come and gone. But for me, there is no need to try and explain everything here again, from my side, from what I know has happened in the past or not.

"I'm just looking into the future and just enjoying my time racing."

title: Adrian Newey issues Honda 'truth' in Red Bull-Aston Martin comparison
excerpt:
Aston Martin's current situation with Honda is not Adrian Newey's first difficult period with the Japanese marque.

Adrian Newey has admitted that Honda's current power unit position with Aston Martin is behind where Red Bull found the Japanese manufacturer when the two parties first linked up in 2019.

Honda returned to Formula 1 as a power unit supplier for Aston Martin in 2026, taking over from Mercedes, and has endured a difficult start to the sport's new engine era.

Newey, now Aston Martin's managing technical partner and team principal, has drawn a direct comparison with Red Bull's own introduction to Honda power seven years ago, when the Milton Keynes-based team inherited an engine supplier that had already been working through its problems with the long-defunct McLaren partnership.

Asked whether Aston Martin's relationship with Honda echoes how Red Bull's started back in 2019, Newey told select media, including RacingNews365, that there was a key difference in timing.

"I would say, at the moment, in all truth, that Honda are a little bit behind where Red Bull, as the works team, RBR, picked up Honda in 2019, but that obviously was four seasons after they first came back in 2015," said Newey.

"So this is the first year back in. Repeating myself, they're a great company. I have every confidence that they will accelerate quickly and understand the problems of these particular PU regulations."

'Too early' for Honda 2027 performance prediction

Honda is already working hard on trying to get things right for its power unit next year, with Aston Martin not being able to afford another campaign of fighting at the back.

Newey was reluctant to put a number on the current gap between Aston Martin's chassis and Honda's power unit, pointing instead to publicly available data as the clearer measure.

"So I think the relative deficit between chassis and engine, I think, again, it's probably not for me to say," Newey added. "I think if people look at the GPS, then you can start to get a much better picture from that."

Turning to Honda's longer-term trajectory under the 2026 regulations, which remain in place through the following campaign, Newey said there were reasons for optimism further down the line.

"And then, moving forward to 2027, that's really as we discussed earlier. Honda, there's a lot of energy and projects on the way now that perhaps are in their early stages of development, but we see a lot of promise from those.

"It's too early to comment on exactly where the PU will be at the start of next season, and whether then, assuming it's allowed under the PUAC, there will be further development for what will be race eight at the end of the first period."

title: Kimi Antonelli makes important point over Austin F1 track limits battle
excerpt:
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli believes the nature of the Austin F1 track is adding further complications for drivers in their battle against track limits.

Across Friday practice of the United States Grand Prix, a total of 207 laps were deleted for track limit violations as drivers struggled to stay within the white lines of the bumpy circuit.

Antonelli, who finished in second place in FP2, 0.042s behind pace-setter Charles Leclerc, has had an ongoing battle with track limits himself at times in 2026, and was fortunate to escape a five-second penalty in Singapore - only doing so after Mercedes proved one of his violations came after a technical issue with the brakes.

Turning to the problem at Austin, Antonelli pointed out that the layout of the circuit was, in part, enticing drivers to push further and risk a track limits breach.

"It is not easy; it is a difficult track with a lot of elevation changes, and also the wind in some corners is quite odd," Antonelli reflected on his battle with track limits.

"The track limits [violations] mainly come from mistakes; you just lock up a little, and then you go long, but the FIA is trying their best to widen the white lines.

"But it is difficult; it is not easy, and when you try to discover the limit, it is normal that you get [track limits], but it is also the fact that you have so much tarmac.

"In some corners, we have so much tarmac, and the green bit on some of the exits is very grippy, so that also pushes you to use even more track.

"I know it is going to be [an issue as] everyone got a lot of track limits, and it is not easy.

"But that is why in FP3, it is going to be important to find the limit and understand how much you can push in a corner without doing track limits - so it is going to be a thing, but I will try to do my best."

[Article continues below].

Antonelli on Mercedes F1 upgrade

As for Mercedes continuing to try to understand its Sepang upgrade, which is on both cars for the weekend, Antonelli hinted at potential progress, albeit in a narrow window.

"The car felt a bit better, and I think we did a good step compared to FP1, but there is still lots of work to do," he said.

"But it was a good step forward, and we just need to find a little bit more. [The operating window] is still narrow, and it is not easy, especially on a long run with the tyres, but the team is doing a tremendous job trying to understand the package.

"We're starting to see more and starting to understand more, and trying lots of different things just to put the car in a better window, and we're doing a good job, but there is still time to find."

title: Charles Leclerc airs US GP qualifying worry after 'outstanding' Friday
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has called for calm after a dazzling opening day behind the wheel at the Circuit of the Americas on Friday.

Leclerc entered the race weekend on the back of a podium finish last time out in Singapore, which was his first since Belgium in July.

His weekend got off to the best possible start as he topped both FP1 and FP2, and looked convincingly faster than team-mate Lewis Hamilton.

But with Mercedes and Red Bull lingering close behind on the timesheet, Leclerc is wary that it may not be a similar story on Saturday.

"I really hope so, but I also believe that the others will start pushing a bit more their cars as they always do coming quali, so it's going to be tough," Leclerc said.

"It's been a very clean Friday on my side.

"There's more performance in the car, a little bit more, but the others seem to be gaining more than us from Friday to Saturday.

"Seeing the little gap there is, it's not going to be so easy tomorrow."

[Article continues below]

Leclerc pinpoints reason behind strong early form

Ferrari brought upgrades to Austin, primarily on the floor, as it continues to chase performance late into the season.

While Leclerc commended their performance, he suggested Ferrari's strong pace had more to do with getting its balance right early on compared to rival teams.

"It felt good, but as I was saying yesterday, it's really not the gain that I've seen or heard about.

"It's small gains, but it's small gains that we could still see on the car.

"It doesn't feel massively different, but it's a small step forward.

"We also started the weekend on the right foot with a good balance. That is probably the outstanding thing for this Friday."
